<section class="block" id="research">
  <h2 class="section-title">Working papers</h2>

  <article class="paper">
    <h3 class="paper-title">The China Shock and Internal Migration: Evidence from Bilateral Migration Flows<span class="badges"><span class="badge status-submitted">Submitted</span></span></h3>
    <p class="authors"><span class="me">Hyoungchul Kim</span>, <a href="https://sites.google.com/view/jaerimchoi">Jaerim Choi</a>, and <a href="https://sites.google.com/view/seunghoon/home">Seung Hoon Lee</a></p>
    <p class="venue">June 2026.</p>
    <details class="abstract">
      <summary>Abstract</summary>
      <div class="abstract-body">
        Using Korean administrative data spanning nearly two decades and covering the universe of
        bilateral migration flows across local labor markets, we examine how the China trade shock
        shapes internal migration. While prior studies rely on net population changes to measure
        labor adjustment, we exploit bilateral migration flows that separately capture in- and
        out-migration. We find that trade exposure primarily increases out-migration from adversely
        affected regions, with limited effects on in-migration, revealing asymmetric spatial
        adjustment. Decomposing the shock, export expansion reduces out-migration, whereas import
        competition increases it. Migration responses are strongest among prime working-age
        individuals and substantially weaker among younger and older cohorts. Single-person
        households are more responsive than multi-person households. Overall, bilateral data reveal
        substantial migration responses that conventional net population measures fail to detect,
        offering new insight into the &ldquo;missing migration puzzle.&rdquo;
      </div>
    </details>
    <div class="links">
      <a href="research/working-paper/migration_china_shock.pdf">Paper (PDF)</a>
      <a href="https://github.com/hchulkim/research_china-shock-migration">Replication</a>
    </div>
  </article>
